title: Living in Georgia | How People Live in the Country of Europe's Highest Village and Oldest Wine | 4K
fullText: High in the Caucusus Mountains, where two continents lean against each other, there is a village where every house comes with its own thousand-year-old stone tower. Below it, in sunlit valleys, farmers bury clay vessels the size of small cars, fill them with grapes, and let the earth itself make the wine the way their ancestors did 8,000 years ago. And in the evenings, long tables fill with food. Someone stands, raises a glass, and three-part harmonies rise without a single instrument. This is Georgia. Not the American state, the country. A nation of about 3.7 million people wedged between mountains and the Black Sea that most of the world has never seen. Here is what makes this small country impossible to forget. Its language is related to no other language on earth. Its alphabet is so beloved that the nation built a tower in its honor. Archaeologists say wine itself was born here before the pyramids before the wheel reached Europe. And its people survived centuries of invasions without ever taking down the dinner table. Today we cross Georgia from a capital built on hot springs to the highest village in Europe. Chasing one question, how does a nation this small hold on to so much for so long? In Georgia, they say every guest is a gift from God. Stay with us to the end. Tonight, the guest is you. Legend says Tibilisi began with a hunting trip 15 centuries ago. As the story goes, King Vaktang Gorgasali shot a pheasant above a wooded valley and the bird fell into a hidden spring so hot that it came out cooked. The king took it as a sign and moved his capital here. True or not, the name stuck. Tibelissi means warm place. And the sulfur springs still steam beneath the old town today under brick domes where Georgians have soaked and gossiped for over a thousand years. Walk uphill from the baths and the city shows you how it actually lives. Old Tibeli is a maze of wooden balconies leaning over narrow lanes. And behind the gates lie its real treasure, the courtyards. Strung with laundry lines and grape vines, they work like shared living rooms. Neighbors drink coffee at a common table. Children ride bicycles between staircases. And an argument on the second floor is public property by dinnertime. Nobody in these courtyards is ever entirely alone, which is exactly how they like it. Mornings belong to the bizaar. The air is a braid of smells. Fresh cilantro and tagon, barrels of pickled vegetables, wheels of salty sulani cheese, potatoes still wearing their soil. Vendors press samples into your hands whether you intend to buy or not. Haggling here is not a battle. It is a conversation with a discount at the end and regular customers are greeted like returning family. The city wears its history in layers. A sixth century church stands a short walk from a Soviet apartment block which stands across the river from a glass bridge that lights up after dark. That bridge, the bridge of peace, does something almost nobody notices. Its thousands of lights flash in a coded rhythm, spelling out a message across the water every night. A modern city quietly talking to itself in light. 19 centuries of invaders have burned this capital to the ground and rebuilt it dozens of times. Persians, Arabs, Mongols, and more as the chronicles count them. Yet the courtyards refill, the springs keep steaming, and the vines grow back over the balconies. To understand the stubbornness underneath all that warmth, you need to hear the language these people refuse to let go of. Listen to Georgian for one minute and you will give up trying to place it. It is not Slavic, not Turkish, not Persian. And it shares no family tree with any of them. Linguists classify Cartelian as its own language group related to nothing else on Earth. While empires pushed their tongues across every border around it, this small nation kept speaking something the rest of the world has never managed to claim. Then there is the way it looks. The Georgian alphabet is a flowing procession of curves. No capital letters, no sharp corners like vines drawn by a careful hand. It first appears in stone inscriptions in the fifth century and Georgians have guarded it through every occupation since. UNESCO lists the living culture of its three historic scripts as heritage of humanity and you can watch the letters dance on every street sign in the country. Few nations celebrate a writing system the way this one does. Georgia holds an official day of honor for its mother tongue and alphabet each spring with flowers laid and speeches given for letters. And on the Black Sea coast, the city of Batumi raised a 130 m steel tower shaped like a strand of DNA wrapped in glowing Georgian characters. Other countries build towers for banks and kings. Georgia built one for its ABCs. The reason runs deep. For a nation invaded from every direction for 2,000 years, the language was the one border no army could cross. Grandmothers taught the letters when schools were forbidden to. Monks copied manuscripts by candle light in mountain monasteries while empires rose and fell below. Every child who learns to write those curving letters today is in a quiet way winning a war that never quite ended. A visitor only needs one word to open every door in the country. Gama jo it literally carries the old root of victory. So even a morning greeting here is a small celebration of survival. But if you want to see the Georgian language in its full glory, you do not go to a library. You go to a table. Sooner or later, everyone in Georgia is invited to a supra. And it is not a dinner party. It is a ceremony with its own laws older than most parliaments. The table is loaded until the plates stack on top of each other. Cheese filled kacapuri bread, steaming kinkali dumplings, walnut sauces, herbs by the fistful and wine in clay pitches. But food is not the point. The supra is a structure built out of words and one man is responsible for the architecture. He is called the tomato, the toastmaster. And Georgians will tell you a good one is worth more than a good cook. A tomato must be part historian, part poet, part philosopher, and part referee. He sets the rhythm of the entire evening, raising themes one by one in an order polished by centuries. To peace, to the homeland, to parents, to children, to friendship. Each toast is not a sentence, but a small speech, and guests answer with stories of their own. No one drinks between toasts. The glass waits for the words. Then somewhere past the third toast, it happens. Three men at the table lean together and begin to sing. Three separate melodic lines, no instruments, weaving over and under each other in harmonies that raise the hair on your arms. This is Georgian polifany. And when UNESCO created its very first list of humanity's living cultural treasures in 2001, this singing was on it. Scholars believe these harmonies may be older than the polifany of Western Europe. At the table, nobody is thinking about scholars. They are simply singing the way this land has always sung. And then comes the toast that silences the room. At every true supra, the tomato eventually raises his glass to those who are gone. The chairs slide back, everyone stands, and for a long moment, the loudest table in the world goes completely quiet. Grandfathers are named, old friends are remembered. In Georgia, the dead are not absent from the feast. They have a standing invitation. There is a saying here that explains all of it. Every guest is a gift from God. It is not a slogan on a souvenir mug. It is a rule people actually live by. Travelers discover it the hard way. when a wrong turn down a village road ends 4 hours later at a stranger's table three toasts deep with a bag of walnuts for the journey home. What fills those glasses, of course, deserves a chapter of its own. 20 mi south of Tibelisi rises a modest mound of earth called Gadachrigora. It does not look like the birthplace of anything, but in its soil, archaeologists found pottery shards roughly 8,000 years old, decorated with grape clusters and coated with the chemical fingerprints of fermented grapes. Tartaric acid soaked deep into the clay. It is the oldest evidence of wine- making ever found. Before Egypt raised a pyramid, before writing reached Europe, someone on this hillside was already making wine. More remarkable still, the method never died. Georgians ferment wine in a quevy, a huge egg-shaped clay vessel waxed inside, buried to its neck in the cellar floor. Grapes go in with skins, stems, and all. The earth keeps the temperature steady, and the wine slowly turns a deep amber color that stuns firsttime visitors. In 2013, UNESCO inscribed cavevery wine-making on its list of humanity's intangible heritage, not as history, but as a living practice in thousands of family sellers. Someone has to build those vessels. And in the village of Vardis Sububani in Keti, that someone is Zaza Kabilashi. He is the fourth generation of his family to make cui in a craft he learned from his father Remy who gave more than 40 years to it. Zaza builds each vessel the slow way. Coil after coil of clay, each layer left to dry for days before the next can be added. Months of patience for a single jar. The largest he ever made weighed 2 and 1/2 tons. His children are already learning the trade, which means the count will soon reach five generations. Autumn is when the whole story comes together. In the harvest season, Georgians call RTI. Extended families pour into the kiti vineyards, grandmothers commanding the sorting tables, children riding on trailers of grapes, and by evening the courtyard presses are running while someone inevitably starts a song. It is less an agricultural task than a national holiday that happens to produce wine. Georgians will tell you with a smile that they have a hard time taking wine snobbery seriously. When a sumeier calls amber wine a bold new trend, a Kitian farmer can point at a buried jar and note that his family considered it a new trend about 8,000 years ago. From the warm valleys of wine country, though the road bends north toward a mountain where the air thins and the legends begin. North of Tibeli, the Georgian military highway climbs through gorges that empires have marched down for 2,000 years. And dead ahead, the sky fills with a white pyramid. Mount Kazbeck is a dormant volcano rising over 5,000 m so high it makes its own weather. Villages at its feet spend the morning in sunshine and the afternoon inside a cloud. And nobody plans anything without first looking up. Every great mountain collects stories, but Kazbeck carries one of the oldest on earth. In Georgian epic, a hero named Amirani defied the gods. And as the epic tells it, he was punished by being chained to this very mountain where an eagle returns to tear at him for eternity. If that sounds familiar, it should. The Greeks told the same story about Prometheus. And they placed his punishment in these same Caucusus mountains. Two civilizations, one mountain, one warning about defying heaven. Halfway up its slope stands one of the most photographed sites in the country, the Gergeti Trinity Church. The small 14th century stone chapel sits alone on a bald ridge at 2,170 m dwarfed by the wall of ice behind it. For centuries, when invaders reached the lands, monks are said to have carried the nation's treasures up to this church for safekeeping. The climb that pilgrims once made on foot in hours. Marshutka drivers now rattle up in 20 minutes, and the view at the top silences every van load. The town below the mountain, Stance Minda, lives an ordinary life in an extraordinary place. Children walk to school under a 5,000 m volcano. Guest house owners check the peak each morning the way city people check their phones. Climbers from around the world sought ropes in cafes beside farmers selling honey. And everyone agrees without saying it that the mountain is in charge. Kazbeck, though, is only the doorway to Georgia's high country. Far to the west, deeper and harder to reach, lies a region where the Middle Ages never entirely ended. Where families still live beside the stone towers their ancestors built. a thousand years ago. In the far northwest, pressed against the highest wall of the Caucasus, lies Swaniti. And at its end, the road runs out at a place called Ushkulli. It is a cluster of four stone villages sitting between 2,00 and 2,200 m watched over by Georgia's highest peak at 5,21 m. By most measures, this is the highest continuously inhabited settlement in Europe. People have simply never left. What stops every visitor cold is the skyline. More than 200 medieval stone towers rise above the slate roofs, some dating back to the 9th century. These were not a king's fortresses. They were family towers. Each household kept its own, stocked with food and water, ready for feuds, invaders, or avalanches. When trouble came, the family climbed inside and pulled up the ladder. A thousand years later, the towers still stand beside the houses like tall, silent grandparents. And UNESCO has protected the whole region since 1996. The Sans themselves are a story within the story. They speak Swan, a language of their own that even other Georgians cannot understand. Never written down. Passed from kitchen to kitchen for millennia. Their isolation was so complete that historians describes Feneti as the nation's safe. When land, Georgia burned, icons and treasures were carried up here beyond the reach of any army, and the Sans guarded them for centuries. Life at this altitude has never been soft. Winter buries the villages for months, and the single road to Ushkulli can vanish under snow, leaving the community to its own devices. Firewood, potatoes, salted cheese, and patience. And yet, the school stays open for its handful of children. Cows wander the lanes, past thousand-year-old towers, and grandmothers sell knitted socks to the summer hikers. Ask a Swan why the family never moved somewhere easier, and you get a look that suggests the question does not translate. In summer, the meadows around the towers turn so green and thick with wild flowers that the hardness almost hides itself. Almost. Because to reach Georgia's other high refuge on the opposite end of the mountains, you must first survive the road there. And that road has a reputation all its own. In the far northeast, one dirt road connects the region of Tuscetti to the rest of the country, and it goes over the Abano Pass at roughly 2,800 m, about 9,300 ft. There are no guard rails. The track is carved straight into the cliffside wide enough for one vehicle often wrapped in fog with a drop below that travel writers have run out of adjectives for. It is regularly ranked among the most dangerous roads in Europe and it is the only way in. The pass is open just a few months a year. When the first serious snowfalls, Tuscetti closes like a book, and it does not reopen until summer. For centuries, this rhythm shaped a way of life found almost nowhere else. The villages up here were never year round homes, but summer capitals. Families returned each June like migrating birds, reopening houses, repairing towers, and pasturing their flocks on the high meadows. The flocks are the point. Toshetti is shepherd country, and each summer the sheep come back up the pass the way they have for a thousand years. Thousands of animals flow along the cliffside track in a slow woolly river. Dogs at the edges, shepherds behind. Traffic simply waits because there is no argument to be had with a flock that size. Their milk becomes guda cheese aged in sheepkin the old way, sharp enough to be famous across the country. The villages themselves, Omalo, Shinako, Dartllo, look grown rather than built. Slate roofs, stone towers, balconies weathered to silver. There is little electricity beyond solar panels, no cinema, no mall, and in the summer months, no shortage of people who would not trade it for anywhere. Hikers arrive over the mountains. Families return from the lands and the villages fill with sheep bells and woods until the pass closes again. A road that dangerous closed half the year should have emptied these mountains long ago. Instead, every summer, the people of Tusetti drive it home, which tells you most of what you need to know about how Georgians feel about their high places. The lands, meanwhile, hide wonders of a completely different kind, carved not above the land, but into it. Long before Georgia built towers into the sky, it dug cities into the rock. At Upliki, on a ridge above the Mcvari River, an entire town was carved from stone roughly 3,000 years ago. 150 caves once held temples, wine sellers, a theater, and streets worn smooth by bronze age feet. Caravans on the Silk Road stopped here when Rome was still a village. But the masterpiece is Vardzia. In the 12th century, in the golden age of Queen Tamar, as the chronicles tell it, workers hollowed a secret city into a cliff face. Hundreds of rooms spread across many levels, chapels, bakeries, wine sellers, and tunnels, all hidden behind the mountains, unbroken stone skin. An invading army could ride past and see nothing but rock. Then in the following century, an earthquake sheared the front off the cliff in one catastrophic slice. The secret city was suddenly exposed to the valley. Every room visible at once like a doll's house with its lid torn away. Monks live and pray in a corner of it. To this day, Western Georgia answers with wonders of water. At Mount Villi, a river the color of green glass has cut a canyon so lush it looks prehistoric. Moss dripping from the walls, sunlight falling in shafts through the canopy. For generations, this paradise was private. the bathing spot of the noble Dadani family who came here to escape the summer heat. Today, small boats carry anyone at all between the cliffs, drifting through what a duke once kept for himself. And then there is Tcalubo, the strangest stop of all. In the last century, this spar town was famous for its grand bathouses and sanatoriums built around Raidon Springs that drew the powerful from across a vanished empire. Around 2022 of those palaces now stand abandoned. Marble staircases open to the sky, trees growing through ballroom floors, sunlight pouring into halls where orchestras once played. It is decay so beautiful that photographers cross continents for it and the town around it simply carries on. Cave cities, secret monasteries, noble bathing grounds, haunted spars. Georgia's landscape reads like an attic packed by a family that never threw anything away. But the country's bestkept treasure is not carved in any cliff. It is the price of an ordinary, delicious, unhurried daily life. Morning in a Georgian town starts at the bakery. often a hole in the wall with a round clay oven called a tone sunk into the counter. The baker slaps flat loaves of shies puri against the hot inner walls where they bake while hanging on and pulls them out golden and blistered with a hook. Locals carry them home bare-handed, tossing them from palm to palm because some things are worth a little burning. Lunch is a masterclass in getting rich flavor from a modest bill. Pinkali pleated soup dumplings the size of a fist arrive by the plateful. The rule is to hold the topnot bite carefully and drink the broth before the rest. The top knots left on your plate keep the score. Kacapuri comes in regional versions. The most famous, a bread boat filled with molten cheese, butter, and a barely set egg. None of it is fancy. All of it is serious, and most of it costs less than a coffee in Manhattan. That gentle cost of living has not gone unnoticed. In recent years, remote workers and early retirees from Europe and America have quietly discovered that a comfortable life here, an apartment, fresh markets, fast internet, a mountain view, runs a fraction of what they paid at home. Cafes in Tibilisi now hold a peaceful truce between old men playing back gammon and young foreigners on laptops. And the city hosts both without changing for either. Getting around is its own initiation. The marshutka, a shared minibus, leaves when the driver decides, stops where passengers ask, and connects every village in the country for pocket change. Grandmother's board with cheese wheels, students with guitars, and somewhere on route, a stranger will insist on knowing where you are from and whether you have eaten. Refusing the snack that follows is technically possible and socially unthinkable. On the Black Sea coast, the day ends on the Batumi Boulevard. Families stroll past palm trees. The alphabet tower glows with its spiral of letters, and the mountains you crossed a day ago stand blue on the horizon. Beach in the morning, 5,000 m peaks by nightfall. Few countries fit so much into so little space. Which raises the real question, the one this whole journey has been circling. What keeps a people singing after 2,000 years of trouble? Step back and Georgia's history reads like a list of reasons a nation should not exist. It sits on the land bridge between empires and nearly every one of them Persian, Mongol, Ottoman, and more has marched through, as the chronicles count them, burning capitals and redrawing maps. A people this small in a place this contested should have been absorbed centuries ago. The language should be a footnote. The alphabet should be in a museum. Instead, all of it is still here. And the reasons are the things you have just seen. The towers of Ushkuli stand because every family refused to leave the mountains. The alphabet survives because grandmothers taught it when it was dangerous too. The wine survives because families kept burying in their cellars no matter whose flag flew over Tibilisi. In Vard Sububani, Zaza Kabilashi is teaching his children to coil clay exactly as his greatgrandfather did. And with them, account reaches five generations and the 8,000-year story refuses to end. There is a pattern in how this country defended itself. Other nations survived by building higher walls. Georgia certainly built its share. But what actually carried it through was the table. The Supra turned every occupation into something to outlast. every funeral into a promise of memory, every stranger into a guest, and every guest into a witness. You cannot fully conquer a people who respond to catastrophe by setting more places at dinner. So, the answer to our question turns out to be simple. They stay because leaving would mean putting down the glass. And the glass is never just wine. It holds the dead who are toasted at every feast. The letters monks copied by candle light. The harvest songs in three parts. The tower keys passed from father to son. A Georgian at the table is never only one person. He is everyone who kept the seat warm before him. They do not raise walls against the world. They raise glasses to it. And tonight, somewhere in a courtyard in Tibelisi, under a grape vine older than the government, a tomato is standing up. And the evening's first toast is beginning. To peace, as it always begins. If you listen closely, you are already invited. Thank you for traveling Georgia with us, the country. And now you know the difference. Tell us in the comments. Which moment would you choose, a seat at a Supra or a morning under the towers of Ushkulli? If you have Georgian roots, tell us about your family's table. And if this journey moved you, subscribe. The next hidden country is already waiting.
fullTextVi: Ở trên dãy núi Caucusus, nơi hai lục địa tựa vào nhau, có một ngôi làng nơi mỗi ngôi nhà đều có tháp đá nghìn năm tuổi. Bên dưới nó, trong những thung lũng ngập nắng, những người nông dân chôn những chiếc bình đất sét có kích thước bằng những chiếc ô tô nhỏ, lấp đầy chúng bằng nho và để trái đất tự tạo ra rượu theo cách tổ tiên của họ đã làm cách đây 8.000 năm. Và vào buổi tối, những chiếc bàn dài chứa đầy thức ăn. Ai đó đứng lên, nâng ly và hòa âm ba phần nổi lên mà không cần một nhạc cụ nào. Đây là Georgia. Không phải tiểu bang Mỹ, đất nước. Một quốc gia khoảng 3. 7 triệu người chen chúc giữa những ngọn núi và Biển Đen mà hầu hết thế giới chưa từng thấy. Đây là điều khiến đất nước nhỏ bé này không thể nào quên. Ngôn ngữ của nó không liên quan đến ngôn ngữ nào khác trên trái đất. Bảng chữ cái của nó được yêu thích đến mức cả nước đã xây dựng một tòa tháp để vinh danh nó. Các nhà khảo cổ cho biết rượu vang đã ra đời ở đây trước các kim tự tháp, trước khi bánh xe chạm tới Châu Âu. Và người dân của nó đã sống sót qua nhiều thế kỷ bị xâm lược mà không bao giờ phải ngồi xuống bàn ăn. Hôm nay chúng ta băng qua Georgia từ thủ đô được xây dựng trên suối nước nóng đến đỉnh cao nhất ngôi làng ở châu Âu. Đuổi theo một câu hỏi, làm sao một quốc gia nhỏ bé này lại có thể nắm giữ được nhiều như vậy lâu như vậy? Ở Georgia, người ta nói mỗi vị khách đều là một món quà của Chúa. Ở lại với chúng tôi cho đến cuối cùng. Tối nay khách là bạn. Truyền thuyết kể rằng Tibilisi bắt đầu bằng một chuyến đi săn cách đây 15 thế kỷ. Chuyện kể rằng, Vua Vaktang Gorgasali đã bắn một con gà lôi phía trên một thung lũng đầy cây cối rậm rạp và con chim rơi vào một con suối ẩn nóng đến nỗi nó bật ra nấu chín. Nhà vua coi đó là dấu hiệu và dời đô về đây. Đúng hay không, cái tên vẫn bị mắc kẹt. Tibelissi có nghĩa là nơi ấm áp. Và dòng suối lưu huỳnh ngày nay vẫn còn bốc hơi bên dưới khu phố cổ dưới mái vòm gạch nơi người Georgia đã ngâm mình và buôn chuyện suốt hơn một nghìn năm. Đi bộ lên dốc từ nhà tắm và thành phố sẽ cho bạn thấy nó thực sự tồn tại như thế nào. Old Tibeli là một mê cung với những ban công bằng gỗ nghiêng trên những con đường hẹp. Và đằng sau cánh cổng là kho báu thực sự của nó, những khoảng sân. Được trang bị dây chuyền giặt và dây nho, chúng hoạt động giống như phòng khách chung. Hàng xóm uống cà phê ở bàn chung. Trẻ em đi xe đạp giữa các cầu thang. Và một cuộc tranh luận trên tầng hai là tài sản công vào giờ ăn tối. Không ai trong những khoảng sân này hoàn toàn cô đơn, đó chính xác là cách họ thích it. Buổi sáng thuộc về bizaar. Không khí là một dải mùi. Ngò và tagon tươi, thùng rau ngâm, bánh phô mai sulani mặn, khoai tây vẫn mặc đất của họ. Người bán hàng sẽ ấn mẫu vào tay bạn dù bạn có ý định mua hay không. Mặc cả ở đây không phải là một trận chiến. Đó là một cuộc trò chuyện có giảm giá ở cuối và khách hàng thường xuyên là chào đón như trở về gia đình. Thành phố mặc lịch sử của nó theo từng lớp. Một nhà thờ thế kỷ thứ sáu nằm cách khu chung cư Liên Xô một quãng đi bộ ngắn đứng bên kia sông từ một cây cầu kính sáng lên khi trời tối. Cây cầu đó, cây cầu hòa bình, làm được một việc mà hầu như không ai để ý. Hàng ngàn ánh sáng của nó nhấp nháy theo nhịp điệu được mã hóa, đánh vần một thông điệp trên nước mỗi đêm. Một thành phố hiện đại lặng lẽ nói chuyện với chính mình trong ánh sáng. 19 thế kỷ quân xâm lược đã đốt trụi thủ đô này và xây dựng lại hàng chục lần. Người Ba Tư, người Ả Rập, người Mông Cổ, và nhiều người khác nữa như được ghi trong biên niên sử. Vậy mà sân vẫn đầy nước, suối vẫn tiếp tục bốc hơi và dây leo mọc lại các ban công. Để hiểu được sự bướng bỉnh bên dưới sự ấm áp đó, bạn cần nghe được ngôn ngữ những người này không chịu buông bỏ. Hãy nghe tiếng Georgian trong một phút và bạn sẽ từ bỏ việc cố gắng đặt it. Khoảng năm 2022, những cung điện đó hiện bị bỏ hoang. Cầu thang bằng đá cẩm thạch mở ra bầu trời, cây cối mọc xuyên qua sàn phòng khiêu vũ, ánh nắng tràn vào hội trường nơi các dàn nhạc từng chơi. Nó đẹp đến mức các nhiếp ảnh gia phải băng qua nhiều châu lục để tìm nó và thị trấn xung quanh nó chỉ đơn giản là tiếp tục. Những thành phố hang động, những tu viện bí mật, những bãi tắm cao quý, những cột đá bị ma ám. Phong cảnh của Georgia trông giống như một căn gác mái được bao bọc bởi một gia đình chưa bao giờ ném bất cứ thứ gì away. Nhưng kho báu được gìn giữ tốt nhất của đất nước không được khắc vào bất kỳ vách đá nào. Đó là cái giá của một cuộc sống thường nhật bình dị, ngon lành, nhàn nhã. Người dân địa phương tay không mang chúng về nhà, ném từ lòng bàn tay này sang lòng bàn tay khác vì một số thứ có giá trị một chút đốt cháy. Bữa trưa là một lớp học bậc thầy để có được hương vị đậm đà từ một hóa đơn khiêm tốn. Bánh bao súp xếp nếp Pinkali có kích thước bằng nắm tay được đặt trên đĩa. Trong những năm gần đây, những người lao động ở xa và những người về hưu sớm ở Châu Âu và Châu Mỹ đã lặng lẽ phát hiện ra rằng cuộc sống thoải mái ở đây, một căn hộ, chợ tươi, internet nhanh, một ngọn núi xem, chạy một phần nhỏ số tiền họ đã trả ở nhà. Và thành phố tổ chức cả hai mà không thay đổi. Đi lại là sự khởi đầu của chính nó. Marshutka, một loại xe buýt nhỏ dùng chung, khởi hành khi tài xế quyết định, dừng khi hành khách hỏi, và kết nối mọi ngôi làng trong nước để kiếm tiền lẻ. Chiếc ván của bà với bánh xe pho mát, học sinh với đàn guitar và đâu đó trên đường, một người lạ sẽ nhất quyết muốn biết bạn đến từ đâu và bạn đã ăn gì chưa.
